newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power higher amid plant outages.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power higher amid plant outages.

text.p: Western U.S. spot power prices moved higher in late morning trade amid talk of another coal-fired power plant outage, trade sources said Tuesday.
"Prices at COB (California-Oregon border) started out around $11.50 (per megawatt hour), but moved up to $13.00 and $14.00 near the end of trade," said one utility source.
He noted that several Northwest utilities were looking to buy power rather than sell, which helped to drive up prices.
Another California trader said the tightness was particulary apparent for morning and evening peaks in the day-ahead market.
Traders cited talk of an outage at the Colstrip coal-fired power plant in Montana, which consists of several units, but the plant's status could not be immediately confirmed.

Restart of a 755 MW unit at the Four Corners coal-fired plant in New Mexico was delayed until Wednesday by the discovery of a boiler tube leak, a spokeswoman for the plant's operator, Arizona Public Service Co, said Tuesday.
The unit, which went down on Sunday, had been expected to restart by noon PST on Tuesday.
The Pacific Northwest was expected to see generally dry and mild weather this week, with temperatures average to slightly above normal, Weather Services Corp said.
Southwest temperatures were expected to be 2 to 8 degrees F below normal through the week.
Wednesday firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) was quoted at $12.50-13.50 per megawatt hour (MWh), compared with $11.25-12.25 for Monday.
Firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) was at $10.50-11.50, while off-peak was at $6.00-7.00.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity was higher at $13.50-14.00, while off-peak was quoted at $7.00-9.00.
Next-day firm, peak power at Four Corners was quoted at $13.00-14.00, while off-peak was at $7.00-9.00.
